title: Facing Death: The Last Enemy and the Sure Hope
subtitle: The one appointment none of us will miss, and a faith honest enough to face it. The ancient art of dying well, the fear under the fear, and the Christian hope that is not a vague afterlife but a raised body in a remade world.

connections.label: Suffering and the Silence of God
The Anxious Mind: Faith and Mental Health

parts.title: The Appointment You Have Already Made
parts.body:
You are going to die. Not as a doctrine, not as a someday, but as a fact already scheduled, the one appointment you will keep without fail, and somewhere underneath the busyness of an ordinary Tuesday you know it, which is exactly why you keep the busyness running. The thought arrives at the wrong hours. A scan you are waiting on. A parent in a hospital bed who has started to look like a country you will soon have to leave. A birthday with a number on it that you did not expect to mind. And for a moment the floor of the ordinary day goes thin, and you can see straight through it to the thing under everything, and then you reach for your phone, because the modern world has built a thousand exits from this one thought.

We are the first society in human history to have organized itself almost entirely around not seeing death. Our ancestors watched people die in the front room. We move the dying to the hospital and the dead to the funeral home, and we have so thoroughly outsourced the whole business that most adults have never once been in the room when a person died. We have made death obscene the way the Victorians made sex obscene, the unmentionable subject, the thing you are not supposed to bring up at dinner. And the cost of all this hiding is not less fear. It is more, a low dread with no language, a terror we have no rituals to hold.

Maybe the church did not help. Maybe you got a Christianity that talked about heaven so vaguely it sounded like a consolation prize, wings and clouds and an eternity of disembodied harp music that no honest person actually wants. Maybe you got the opposite, a faith so focused on getting souls to heaven that it forgot the body entirely, as if the goal were to escape creation rather than to see it raised. Either way you were left without what you most need, which is not a distraction from death and not a daydream about death, but a way to face it with your eyes open.

Let me say the thing the modern world has tried to make unsayable. Death is real, it is an enemy, and it is also not the end of the story. The Christian faith does not ask you to pretend death is a friend or a doorway or a natural part of the circle of life. It calls death the last enemy. And then it makes a claim so large that if it is true, nothing is the same. It claims that this enemy has already been defeated, in a real death and a real resurrection, and that yours is coming too. You do not have to look away anymore. There is something here strong enough to be looked at.

parts.title: Why Facing It Changes Everything
parts.body:
It matters because the fear of death, even unexamined, runs the engine of a great deal of human misery. The writer of Hebrews says it plainly, that people are held in lifelong slavery by their fear of death, and the modern world is a vast machine for managing that fear without naming it. The frantic accumulation, the desperate clinging to youth, the inability to be still, the way we treat aging as a disease to be defeated rather than a season to be lived, all of it is, at bottom, a flight from the one appointment. A person who has never faced death is run by it, and does not know it.

It matters because how you die is part of how you live, and the two cannot be separated. The ancients understood that dying well is not a separate skill from living well but its final exam, and a culture that cannot talk about death produces people who cannot prepare for it, who arrive at the end unready, with the important things unsaid and the relationships unmended and the soul unsettled. We medicalize the end so thoroughly that we often miss the chance to die as a human being rather than as a failing set of organs, surrounded by machines instead of by the people and the words and the God we need.

It matters for the church's witness, because the watching world reads us most carefully at deathbeds and gravesides. When a Christian dies in peace, not in denial but in genuine, eyes-open peace, having faced the worst the world can do and found it already conquered, the skeptic sees something no argument could supply. The early church grew, in part, because Christians died differently, and the pagan world noticed. A faith that cannot face death is not worth much, because death is the test every faith eventually sits. A faith that can face it is the most persuasive thing in the world.

And it matters because you love people, and everyone you love will die, and so will you, and the love that refuses to reckon with this is a love that will be ambushed. Learning to face death, your own and theirs, is not morbid. It is the condition of loving anyone honestly in a world where the parting is built in. The people who have made peace with their mortality are not the gloomy ones. They are, strangely, the most alive people in the room, because they have stopped pretending they have forever and started receiving each day as the gift it actually is.

parts.title: What Scripture Promises Beyond the Grave
parts.body:
The Bible does not flinch from death, and you should not let anyone tell you it does. It calls death an enemy. The last enemy to be destroyed is death, Paul writes, which means it is not a friend, not a natural good, not the gentle close of a circle. It is an intruder in a world that was made for life, the wage of sin, the great undoing. Scripture grieves death honestly. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus though he was minutes from raising him, because the right response of love to death is tears, even when you hold the cure. Christianity gives you full permission to hate death. It does not ask you to make peace with the enemy.

But then it makes a claim that changes the weight of everything. Christ has been raised from the dead, Paul says, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. The resurrection of Jesus is not presented as a beautiful symbol or a spiritual metaphor. It is presented as an event, in history, attended by witnesses, the hinge on which the whole faith turns, so much so that Paul says if it did not happen, the Christians are to be pitied above all people. And the resurrection of Jesus is offered not as a one-time exception but as the pattern, the firstfruits, the first sheaf of a harvest that includes you. Because he was raised, you will be raised. Death has been defeated not in theory but in a particular tomb outside Jerusalem that was found empty on a particular morning.

And notice precisely what the Christian hope is, because the church has often gotten it fuzzy. The hope is not that your soul floats off to a disembodied heaven forever. That is closer to Plato than to Paul. The Christian hope is resurrection, the raising of the body, and beyond it a remade creation, a new heaven and a new earth where God dwells with his people. There is an intermediate state, to be sure, to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and that is real comfort. But it is the waiting room, not the destination. The destination is your own body, raised and glorified and incorruptible, in a world made new, where the dwelling place of God is with man and he will wipe away every tear from their eyes and death shall be no more. The Christian does not hope to escape creation. The Christian hopes for creation healed.

This is why Paul can taunt the enemy. O death, where is your victory. O death, where is your sting. He is not whistling past the graveyard. He is standing on the far side of an empty tomb, looking back at the thing that terrifies the whole human race, and telling it that its reign is over. The sting of death is sin, he says, and the strength of sin is the law, but thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Death is still an enemy. It is now a defeated one, and the difference between an undefeated enemy and a defeated one is the difference between dread and hope. The Christian dies, but the Christian dies toward something. The grave is real, and it is not the last word, because the One who walked out of his own grave has promised to come back for you.

parts.title: The Lost Art of Dying Well
parts.body:
The church once had an entire body of wisdom devoted to dying, and we have almost completely forgotten it. In the wake of the Black Death, which killed perhaps a third of Europe in the middle of the fourteenth century, the church produced a body of writing called the Ars Moriendi, the Art of Dying. These were practical manuals, widely copied and later printed, that walked an ordinary person through the temptations of the deathbed, despair, loss of faith, impatience, pride, and the clinging to worldly things, and that taught the dying and those around them how to meet the end in hope. The point was that dying well is a skill, that it can be prepared for, and that a good death is the natural fruit of a life rightly ordered toward God.

This was not morbid. It was the opposite. The medieval Christian kept death visible on purpose, in the memento mori, the reminder that you must die, carved into clocks and painted into portraits and prayed in the daily office. Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return, the church says on Ash Wednesday, drawing the cross in ashes on the foreheads of the living. Not to frighten them. To free them. The person who has faced their death is free from the tyranny of death in a way the person who hides from it never is. The monks kept a skull on the desk. The Puritans wrote whole volumes on holy dying. Jeremy Taylor's The Rule and Exercises of Holy Dying, published in 1651, taught a generation that the way to die well is to live well, daily, in view of the end.

The early Christians had already shown the world a new way to die. The Romans burned their dead outside the city walls and regarded a corpse as pollution. The Christians buried their dead with tender care, facing east toward the sunrise, and called the burial grounds koimeteria, dormitories, sleeping places, because they believed the dead were not destroyed but asleep, waiting for a morning. The word itself was a sermon. And the martyrs died singing. When the church watched its own people go to the lions and the fire with a peace the empire could not comprehend, the empire took notice, and many were converted not by Christian arguments but by Christian deaths.

The church carried this wisdom for centuries and then, in the modern West, set it down. The dying were moved from the home to the institution, the dead from the parlor to the mortuary, and within a couple of generations a civilization that had always kept death in view managed to push it almost entirely out of sight. The recovery, where it is happening, is coming partly from an unexpected quarter, the hospice movement, founded by Cicely Saunders, a Christian, who insisted that the dying are living until they die and deserve presence, dignity, and the relief of pain rather than the false war of machines. She was, in a sense, reviving the Ars Moriendi for a secular age. The church should recognize its own inheritance and take it back, because no one knows how to die well anymore, and we used to be the people who taught it.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Death has been studied by doctors, psychologists, and philosophers, and the believer can learn from all of them without fear. All truth is God's truth, and honest observers of the deathbed have seen real things the church should receive. What follows takes several bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each gets right, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of death carries a hidden picture of what a human being is and where they are going, and the picture is where the matter is decided.

secular.author: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross
secular.whatItGetsRight: Kübler-Ross broke a long cultural silence by sitting with the dying and letting them speak, and she gave the world a vocabulary for the emotional terrain of dying, the denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance she observed. Whatever the later corrections, she did something the modern West desperately needed. She walked back into the room with the dying that we had all walked out of, and she insisted that they were people with something to say, not problems to be managed.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Her great limit is the destination she points toward, acceptance, a making of peace with death as the final and healthy stage. Scripture refuses to make peace with death itself. Death is an enemy, the last to be destroyed, and the believer is free to accept the loss of this life without ever accepting death's legitimacy. The Christian aims not at acceptance but at hope, which is a different and stronger thing, the settled trust that the enemy at the door has already been defeated, so that one can face death squarely without surrendering to it as the natural end.

secular.author: Atul Gawande
secular.whatItGetsRight: Gawande, a surgeon, indicted his own profession for waging a futile and often cruel war on death in the final months of life, trading the dying person's actual priorities for a few more weeks of suffering on machines. He argues for hospice, for honest conversations about what matters at the end, for letting people die as people rather than as medical battlegrounds. It is a deeply humane book that recovers much of what the church once knew about the good death.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Gawande sees clearly that a death surrounded by machines is often a worse death than one surrounded by loved ones, and Scripture agrees that how a person dies matters and that presence is better than false war. Where his account stops is at the horizon. Gawande can help you die comfortably and on your own terms. He cannot tell you whether there is anything on the other side of the door, and his wisdom, real as it is, is finally a wisdom for managing an ending. Christianity claims the ending is a beginning, that the body laid down is a seed to be raised, which is the one thing medicine cannot examine and the one thing the dying most need to hear.

secular.author: Ernest Becker
secular.whatItGetsRight: Becker argued, with great force, that the fear of death is the hidden engine of human culture, that nearly everything we build, the empires and the art and the frantic projects of significance, is a defense against the terror of our own annihilation, an attempt to feel that we will not simply vanish. He saw, as few have seen, how much of human life is a flight from this one fact, and how the denial distorts everything it touches.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Becker is doing secular exegesis of a verse he never read, that people are held in lifelong slavery by their fear of death. He diagnoses the slavery with brilliance and has no key for the cell. His conclusion is essentially tragic, that we must build our heroic illusions knowing they are illusions, because there is no actual escape from death to be had. Scripture agrees with the diagnosis entirely and then says the thing Becker could not, that the slavery has an end, that the fear can be broken not by a braver illusion but by a true resurrection. Becker proves we need exactly what the gospel claims to provide, and then, heartbreakingly, denies it is there.

secular.source: The hospice and palliative care movement
secular.author: Cicely Saunders and successors
secular.whatItGetsRight: Saunders built modern hospice on the conviction that the dying are living until they die, that pain can and should be relieved, and that a person at the end deserves presence, dignity, and the freedom to attend to what actually matters. The movement has recovered, in clinical practice, an ancient Christian instinct, that the deathbed is holy ground and the dying are to be accompanied rather than abandoned or assaulted with futile treatment.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: There is little here to correct, because Saunders was herself a Christian recovering the church's own lost wisdom, and Scripture wholly affirms the relief of suffering and the honoring of the dying. The only caution is that palliative care, at its best, manages the dying well and is not itself the hope. A comfortable death is a mercy. A defeated death is the gospel. The believer wants both, the skilled hand that relieves the pain and the sure word that the grave is not the end, and the church should be grateful for the first while never letting it substitute for the second.

secular.author: The philosophy of a finite life
secular.whatItGetsRight: A serious strand of secular thought, from the ancient Epicureans to modern writers, argues that mortality should not be feared because death is simply the absence of experience, and that a finite life can be lived well, gratefully, and fully precisely because it ends. There is real maturity in this, a refusal of frantic denial, an insistence on savoring the given days, a dignity in facing the end without illusion. The church has sometimes been less honest about death than these thinkers are.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Ecclesiastes would shake hands with much of this, the call to receive your bread and your work and your love as gifts precisely because you cannot keep them, the refusal to pretend you have forever. But the secular account asks you to find this peace while believing that you and everyone you love will be utterly and permanently erased, that the love that made the loss matter was pointing at nothing. Scripture says the finitude is real and the erasure is not, that the One who made you for life has defeated the death that ends it. The secular thinker faces the void bravely. The believer faces the same darkness and finds it is not a void but a door, and behind it, a face.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same hope of resurrection still differ on how to face the actual process of dying, and the difference is serious and pastoral. It runs to how far we should go in using medicine to extend life, and where the line falls between fighting death as the enemy it is and surrendering to it as the appointment it is. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are honoring something true, and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: Life is a gift to be guarded, and we fight for it to the end
views.body: This view begins with the conviction that life is a sacred gift from God, that we are stewards and not owners of it, and that the duty to preserve life runs all the way to the edge. Death is an enemy, and one does not lie down before an enemy. Advocates hold that every day of life is a day God has given, that the dying are not less valuable for being near the end, and that the modern temptation to give up early, to call a life no longer worth sustaining, is a door that opens onto terrible places, the quiet pressure on the sick and the old to get out of the way, the redefining of some lives as not worth living. They point to the church's long and costly history of caring for the dying that the world discarded, the plague nurses, the hospitals Christians built, and they insist that the burden of proof lies with stopping treatment, not continuing it. They are guarding against a real danger, a culture that has grown impatient with weakness, that increasingly treats death as a solution and the dependent as a problem, and that can dress its abandonment of the vulnerable in the language of dignity. Against that, they hold the high view of every human life as the image of God to its last breath, and they would rather err on the side of fighting too long than on the side of surrendering a life that God still called good.

views.view: Death is a defeated enemy we need not war against forever
views.body: This view begins with the same conviction that life is a sacred gift, and draws a different conclusion about its end. Because death has already been defeated in Christ, the believer is freed from the desperate, machine-bound war against it that grips a world with no hope beyond the grave. There comes a point, advocates hold, where continued aggressive treatment is no longer stewardship of life but only the prolonging of dying, and where the faithful act is to stop fighting the body and start preparing the soul. They distinguish, carefully, between killing and allowing to die, between hastening death, which they reject, and accepting that one's hour has come, which the saints have always done with peace. They point to a long Christian tradition of the good death, the dying believer who refuses the last futile intervention in order to die surrounded by prayer and family rather than tubes and alarms. They are guarding against a real danger too, an idolatry of mere biological survival that treats death as the ultimate evil to be resisted at any cost, which is precisely the fear-driven posture of people who have no resurrection hope. Against that, they hold that the Christian, of all people, can let go when the time comes, can decline the last desperate measure, and can die toward the One who conquered death rather than clinging to a life that was always meant to be laid down.

parts.title: What the Awareness of Death Forms
parts.body:
Teach us to number our days, the psalmist prays, that we may get a heart of wisdom. There is the whole thing in one sentence. The awareness of death is not meant to terrify you into paralysis. It is meant to wake you up, and the God who keeps the dark fact of mortality in front of his people is forming in them things that the illusion of endless time always prevents.

He forms a freedom from the tyranny of the trivial. The person who has truly faced their own death stops being run by a thousand small fears and false urgencies, because they have looked at the largest fear and found it answered, and everything smaller has shrunk to its proper size. The opinion of strangers, the accumulation of things you cannot take with you, the frantic management of a reputation that the grave will erase, all of it loosens its grip on a person who has numbered their days. The memento mori was never about gloom. It was about clarity, the clarity of someone who has stopped pretending and started living deliberately, with the end in view.

He forms a strange capacity for joy in ordinary things. This is the part that surprises people. You would think that keeping death in view would darken life, and instead it brightens it, because the person who knows the bread is daily, who knows they cannot keep the morning light or the face across the table or the body that still works, receives all of it as gift rather than as entitlement. Ecclesiastes teaches exactly this hard freedom, the freedom of a creature who has stopped trying to wring eternity out of things that were only ever meant to be daily, and who can therefore actually taste them. The dying, and those who have faced dying, are often the most awake people in the room, the ones who notice, who say the thing, who are present in a way the rest of us, who think we have forever, almost never manage.

And he forms hope, which is the deepest formation of all, because hope is not optimism. Optimism expects this life to keep going. Hope expects that even when this life ends, as it will, the story does not. The believer who has faced death and laid hold of the resurrection carries a hope that does not depend on the scan coming back clear, a hope that can stand at a graveside and weep honestly and still say, with Paul, O death, where is your sting. That hope is forged, not felt. It is built by years of facing the enemy and refusing to look away, until a person can say with the old confidence that to live is Christ and to die is gain, and mean it, not as a slogan but as the settled posture of someone who has made friends with their mortality because they have made peace with the One who defeated it.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Facing death is not a one-time achievement but a practice, returned to over a lifetime, and most of it is the slow work of letting an honest awareness of the end reshape an ordinary day. Two things before the list. First, if you are facing a terminal diagnosis or accompanying someone who is, seek out hospice and palliative care early, not late. These are gifts, skilled people who know how to relieve suffering and honor the dying, and using them is wisdom, not surrender. Second, and read this twice. If the weight of mortality, or grief, or despair has brought you to the edge, if you are thinking about ending your life, call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the United States, right now, and tell someone who loves you. Your life is not yours to end. It is a gift God is not finished giving.

steps: Sit with the fact of your own death for ten minutes without reaching for a distraction. Pray Psalm 90, teach us to number our days, and let it do its slow work. Facing it once on purpose breaks some of its power to ambush you.

Say the thing you have been leaving unsaid. Call the parent, the estranged friend, the person you love and have not told. We die with too many words unspoken because we act as though there will always be more time. Act as though there will not.

Read one resurrection passage out loud, 1 Corinthians 15, or John 11, or Revelation 21 from verse 1. Let the actual Christian hope, the raised body and the remade world, replace whatever vague cloud-and-harp picture you inherited.

Notice one ordinary gift today and receive it as a gift, the light, the meal, the face across the table, knowing you cannot keep it. The awareness of death is meant to wake you to the day, not darken it.

Put your affairs in order as an act of love, not morbidity. A will, an advance directive, your wishes written down. Sparing the people you love a fog of decisions in their grief is one of the kindest things you can do, and the doing of it will settle your own mind.

Talk with your family, plainly and without drama, about how you want to die and be buried, what you believe is on the other side, and what you hope for them. The silence around death is broken in conversations exactly this concrete.

Visit someone who is dying, or grieving, and simply be present, the way Job's friends were right for seven days before they ruined it by speaking. Sitting with the dying is how the church learns to die.
Read one short account of a faithful death, a saint, a martyr, a believer who died in hope, and let it teach you that this can be done well, that people have walked through this door singing.

Recover a rhythm that keeps death honestly in view, an annual reading of Ecclesiastes, the practice of Ash Wednesday, a regular visit to a grave. Not to be gloomy. To be free, with the freedom of someone who has stopped pretending they have forever.

Build your hope on the resurrection of Jesus as an event, not a feeling, by studying the case for the empty tomb until you can rest your weight on it. The Christian hope is only as strong as that morning was real, and it was real.

Become the kind of friend who can be present at deathbeds, who does not flee the room, who can sit in the silence and hold a hand and say the true thing softly. The church needs people who have made peace with mortality enough to accompany others through it.

Mend what you would not want to leave broken. Forgive the person, repair the relationship, settle the old account. A good death is the fruit of a life put right, and the time to put it right is while you still have it.

Live deliberately toward the end you know is coming, asking each year what you would stop wasting your life on and what you would start receiving if you truly believed your days are numbered, because they are, and a numbered day is a precious one.

Teach the next generation how to face death, by not hiding it from them, by letting children see grief and burial and honest hope, so that they are not the unprepared adults the modern world keeps producing.

Make your peace with God the central business of your life, not a deathbed afterthought, because the way to die well is to live well now, daily, in view of the One who defeated the grave. The Ars Moriendi was always really an art of living.

Hold the two truths together to the end, that death is a real enemy worth grieving and a defeated enemy worth facing without fear, until you can say with the church across twenty centuries that to live is Christ and to die is gain, and walk through the door when it comes, toward the One who walked through it first and came back to show you the way.
